\# Task: admission gate for 25 screened candidate(s)

Research topic: \*\*empirical reply-to-proposition alignment in email and dialogue, focusing on partial replies, multiple questions, unanswered questions, and multi-proposition antecedents\*\*

Decide which of these candidates enters the reading round. Admit a paper only
when it materially strengthens one of the research streams below, and the
abstract shows that, not merely shared vocabulary. A paper count is never a
reason to admit: admitting six of twenty is a valid answer, and so is
admitting none. Rejecting a paper here costs little; reading a paper that
cannot strengthen a stream costs a reading slot that a better paper needed.

Research streams:
\- F1 [DIRECT] Non-nominal, abstract, and propositional anaphora: Resolve an expression or response to an antecedent denoting a proposition, fact, event, situation, discourse segment, or other non-nominal abstract object. Search terminology must include non-nominal anaphora and non-nominal antecedent because these are important umbrella terms missing from the original seed list.
\- F2 [DIRECT] Dialogue discourse attachment and response relations: Identify which earlier discourse unit a current conversational contribution attaches to and classify the semantic or pragmatic relation between them, including response, acknowledgment, correction, continuation, explanation, question-answer, and related relations.
\- F3 [DIRECT] Question-answer attachment, answerhood, QUD, and unresolved questions: Determine which prior question or issue a response addresses, whether it fully or partially answers that question, and which questions in a multi-question context remain unresolved. Include question-under-discussion and issue-based dialogue terminology rather than relying on generic conversational QA.
\- F4 [DIRECT] Agreement, disagreement, acceptance, rejection, and grounding with explicit targets: Detect acceptance, agreement, rejection, disagreement, confirmation, correction, acknowledgment, or clarification while identifying the proposition or discourse unit that is the target of that act.
\- F5 [DIRECT] Workplace email and enterprise-dialogue response semantics: Empirical studies of replies, communicative acts, requests, decisions, acknowledgments, approvals, and related response behavior in authentic organizational email, meetings, or enterprise chat, searched specifically for antecedent or scope annotations.
\- F6 [DIRECT] Antecedent annotation and span-level response-target evaluation: Annotation schemes and evaluation methods in which a response or anaphor is linked to an exact antecedent span or discourse unit and where null, ambiguous, partial, multiple, or discontinuous targets can be represented rather than forcing a single whole-message antecedent.
\- F7 [TRANSFER] Composite, multiple, split, and discontinuous antecedents: Reference phenomena in which an anaphor or response depends on more than one antecedent unit, a composite discourse referent, a plural or split antecedent, or non-contiguous source material.
\- F8 [TRANSFER] Ambiguous, null, unsupported, and missing antecedents with abstention: Resolution frameworks that represent non-anaphoric cases, absent antecedents, unresolved references, ambiguous antecedent sets, confidence, selective prediction, or abstention rather than always forcing an antecedent.
\- F9 [TRANSFER] Target-conditioned stance and proposition-pair inference: Classify support, contradiction, agreement, rejection, or stance relative to an explicit target proposition, claim, or span once a candidate target has been identified.
\- F10 [TRANSFER] Conversation disentanglement and reply-to graph prediction: Identify which previous message or turn a new conversational message replies to in interleaved or asynchronous conversations.

Open gaps this round must close (a paper that speaks to one of these
is worth admitting even when its topic wording is unusual):
\- gap-1 [ACADEMIC, HIGH]: Direct empirical evidence is still missing for proposition-level agreement, rejection, approval, clarification, and answer scope in authentic workplace email or enterprise chat, especially cases where one short response applies to only part of a preceding message.
    suggested query: "reply scope" email dialogue proposition agreement approval rejection workplace communication
    searched in rounds: [1] (still open)
\- gap-2 [ENGINEERING, HIGH]: The corpus does not establish a validated annotation and evaluation scheme for mapping workplace responses to exact proposition or span targets while representing exact, partial, ambiguous, unsupported, discontinuous, and potentially multiple antecedents.
\- gap-3 [ACADEMIC, HIGH]: Direct evidence remains insufficient for aligning replies to one or more questions when a preceding workplace message contains multiple questions, requests, or alternatives, including detection of questions that remain unanswered.
    suggested query: "question answer alignment" dialogue "multiple questions" partial answer unanswered questions
    searched in rounds: [1] (still open)
\- gap-4 [ACADEMIC, MEDIUM]: It remains open whether and how a workplace response should be modeled as targeting a composite or multi-proposition antecedent. The corpus supports composite abstract discourse referents theoretically and multi-antecedent entity reference analogically, but provides no direct evaluation of multi-proposition reply scope in work communication.
    suggested query: "multi-antecedent" propositional anaphora dialogue composite discourse referent reply
    searched in rounds: [1] (still open)
\- gap-5 [ENGINEERING, HIGH]: The appropriate abstention, ambiguity, and missing-antecedent policy for msgloom has not been validated. In particular, the relative cost of an over-broad approval or commitment link versus leaving a link unresolved is a product-risk assumption that requires an explicit cost model and dedicated benchmark rather than being inferred from these papers.
Decisions:
\- ADMIT — name the stream and why the abstract shows the contribution.
\- REJECT — name the reason: topic words match but the capability does not,
  the evidence duplicates a paper already admitted, or the claim is out of
  scope.
\- PENDING — the abstract cannot settle it; say what would.

\`identity: UNCHECKED\` means the host could not confirm the paper's identifier
with the provider. That is not proof the paper is wrong, but prefer a
VERIFIED paper when the two are otherwise equal, and say so in the reason.



\## Project context you must work within

This is the project's own description of the problem, its boundaries,
and the distinctions it needs preserved. It governs what counts as
relevant; the academic task names alone do not.

\# Topic 04 context — Reference resolution and response scope

\## Why this Topic exists

Business communication contains short expressions whose meaning depends on prior propositions, events, proposals, questions, attachments, or specific spans: “this”, “that proposal”, “same as below”, “approved”, “agreed”, “yes”, “not that part”, “see row 4”, “please do the first two”. Entity coreference alone does not solve these cases.

A reply may answer only one of several questions, agree with a proposal but not its condition, approve an amount but not a date, or reject one clause while accepting the rest. If msgloom attaches a response too broadly, it can invent commitments or close work that remains open.

Topic 04 owns \*\*reference resolution to propositional/event/content antecedents and the semantic scope of responses\*\*.

\## Direct handoffs from earlier Topics

Topic 01 hands off semantic reply/partial-agreement scope after it has identified quotation/source spans. Topic 02 hands off semantic response scope after it has identified Topic-related spans. These are explicit boundaries: Topic 04 should use those structural outputs rather than re-research quotation extraction or Topic segmentation.

\## Core research object

Resolve a current expression/response to one or more exact antecedent spans or structured propositions, with uncertainty where needed:

\`\`\`text
response span
   → antecedent proposition/span(s)
   → relation: answer / agreement / rejection / clarification / condition / reference
   → scope: exact, partial, ambiguous, unsupported
\`\`\`

\## Product and phase relevance

This capability affects Phase 1 semantic triage whenever supplied group context contains replies, approvals, and references. Phase 2 may retrieve additional evidence when the antecedent is outside the supplied context or uncertain. Missing antecedents must remain unresolved rather than guessed.

\## Relationships to other Topics

\| Topic | Relationship |
\| --- | --- |
\| 01 | Provides quote/source-span and message relationship evidence; Topic 04 decides semantic response target/scope. |
\| 02 | Provides work-matter span membership; Topic 04 can constrain antecedent candidates to relevant Topic evidence. |
\| 03 | Stable Topic identity narrows historical antecedent candidates across threads/sources. |
\| 05 | Topic 04 determines what an approval/request/commitment applies to; Topic 05 classifies/extracts the action or speech act itself. |
\| 06 | State changes such as approved/revoked depend on correct response scope. |
\| 07 | If the antecedent is missing, Topic 07 can turn the unresolved reference into a targeted evidence need. |
\| 08 | References to tables, screenshots, attachments, cells/pages, or visual regions require Topic 08 grounding. |
\| 10 | General calibration/attribution evaluation belongs to Topic 10; Topic 04 owns domain-specific reference/response correctness. |

\## Key conceptual distinctions

\- Entity coreference ≠ propositional/discourse reference.
\- Quote source ≠ what the response semantically answers.
\- Agreement detection ≠ agreement scope.
\- Question answering ≠ deciding which prior question a reply addresses.
\- A short “yes” may resolve one proposition while leaving other requests open.
\- Unsupported antecedent ≠ absent antecedent; the correct result may be uncertainty.

\## High-value academic terminology

\- discourse deixis; discourse-deictic reference;
\- abstract anaphora; propositional anaphora; event anaphora;
\- anaphora/coreference to events, propositions, facts, situations;
\- conversational coreference; dialogue reference resolution;
\- dialogue discourse parsing; conversational discourse relations;
\- response-to / reply-to discourse relation;
\- question–answer alignment; question resolution; answer scope;
\- partial answer detection; multi-question answering in dialogue;
\- agreement/disagreement detection; stance with target identification;
\- dialogue act / speech-act relation; adjacency pairs;
\- entailment/contradiction relative to a proposition (transfer evidence);
\- reference resolution to document/table/visual objects (handoff to Topic 08).

\## Query families

\- \`"discourse deixis" dialogue resolution\`
\- \`"abstract anaphora" dialogue\`
\- \`"propositional anaphora" conversation\`
\- \`"event anaphora" email dialogue\`
\- \`"dialogue discourse parsing" response relation\`
\- \`"question answer alignment" dialogue multiple questions\`
\- \`"partial answer" dialogue question\`
\- \`agreement target identification dialogue\`
\- \`"agreement scope" conversation\`
\- \`email reply response scope approval\`
\- \`business email partial approval response\`

\## False friends / exclusions

Do not treat these alone as sufficient:

\- named-entity coreference;
\- generic sentiment/stance without target span;
\- Topic 01 quote attribution;
\- Topic 05 speech-act label without antecedent scope;
\- whole-message NLI that cannot locate the affected proposition;
\- answer correctness benchmarks where the antecedent question is supplied as gold and no reference resolution is required.

\## Gap-evaluation guidance

Prioritize gaps that could make msgloom state a broader approval, answer, rejection, or commitment than the evidence supports. Partial-scope errors are decision-critical. Prefer methods/evaluation that return exact antecedent spans, multiple candidate antecedents, or abstention rather than forcing one message-level label. When missing context is the real problem, hand the evidence need to Topic 07 rather than treating it as a reference-model failure.

\## How to use this file

This file is the self-contained research context for this Topic. A future AI research agent should read \*\*this file first\*\*, then \`BRIEF.md\`, then any existing \`CURRENT\_STATUS.md\`, gap decisions, reports, manifests, and prior-round artifacts in this folder. The aim is that an agent given only this Topic folder can reconstruct the project intent, Topic boundary, dependencies, search vocabulary, and gap-prioritization logic without relying on the original ChatGPT conversation.

If the full repository is available, the authoritative product documents remain \`../../docs/design-brief.md\`, \`../../docs/design-principles.md\`, \`../../docs/design.md\`, and \`../../docs/phase-roadmap.md\`. This file explains how those product constraints apply to this research Topic; it does not replace or approve changes to those design documents.

\## Shared msgloom background

msgloom is a personal work-information system for one user. It is intended to process very large daily volumes of work communication, initially Outlook email and Microsoft Teams, while ensuring that \*\*work requiring the user's response is not missed\*\* and reducing how much the user must read to stay current.

The product is organized around \*\*Topics\*\*, not message summaries. A Topic is a concrete work matter described by information from one or more sources. One message can contain several Topics; one Topic can span many messages, conversations, attachments, groups, and eventually multiple sources. A conversation or Group is therefore not automatically one Topic.

The report contract is the ultimate product pressure on all ten research Topics. Reports must preserve every due Topic and the decision-relevant information needed to act on it, including developments, actions, deadlines, conditions, risks, uncertainty, and links back to exact source evidence. Missing or conflicting information must remain visible rather than being silently filled in.

The design decision order is important when evaluating research gaps: user permissions are fixed; then preserve correct meaning and report coverage; then traceability and recovery; then usability/maintenance; finally speed, brevity, and token savings. A method that is faster but loses a condition, deadline, branch, source relation, or important Topic is not an improvement for msgloom.

Important persistent principles:

\- Use deterministic code for reliable mechanical relationships and AI for language understanding/judgement.
\- Preserve source bytes, versions, stage history, identities, and lineage. New assessments do not erase old evidence.
\- Group only on reliable relationships. Similar subjects, participants, wording, or model labels are not enough to prove Topic identity.
\- Keep uncertain relationships separate and make the reason for uncertainty visible.
\- Brevity must come from concise wording and layered detail, never from omitting decision-essential information.
\- User-reviewed examples, missed important work, false alerts, wrong grouping, lost actions/deadlines, and evidence that changes a decision matter more than paper count or message throughput.

\## Research-programme relationship

The ten Topics form a dependency network rather than ten independent literature reviews. A useful conceptual flow is:

\`\`\`text
01 source/conversation structure
        ↓
02 within-message Topic spans/membership
        ↓
03 cross-thread/source Topic identity
        ↓
04 reference and response scope
        ↓
05 actions / requests / commitments / decisions
        ↓
06 state / factuality / time / revision
        ↓
07 retrieve missing context when needed
        ↘
08 understand attachments / tables / images
        ↓
09 incremental personalized briefing
        ↓
10 evidence, completeness, calibration, reliability evaluation
\`\`\`

This is not a strict processing pipeline. Several Topics feed each other, and Topic 10 is cross-cutting. The numbering primarily gives a research order and ownership boundary so that one Topic does not silently absorb the whole product problem.

\## Gap-evaluation rules inherited from Topics 01 and 02

The Research Pipeline must evaluate gaps using \*\*project value\*\*, not just academic novelty. The following rules are part of the context for every Topic:

1\. A machine-classified \`HIGH\` or \`ACADEMIC\` gap does \*\*not\*\* automatically authorize another literature round.
2\. After each academic round, perform a human/project-value review: decide whether the uncertainty is best addressed by more papers, engineering experiments, a later Topic, production-domain data, candidate-method selection, or no further current work.
3\. Prefer targeted academic follow-up over broad searching. Do not fill paper quotas with weakly related literature.
4\. Distinguish direct target-domain evidence from transfer methods/evaluation evidence. Transfer evidence can justify a mechanism or experiment, not production-email accuracy.
5\. Engineering validation may use independent synthetic/adversarial fixtures and public data. Lack of production mailbox examples is not a reason to stop work that can be validly completed without them.
6\. Never claim production representativeness from synthetic or transfer evidence. Record it as deferred until suitable authorized domain data exists.
7\. If a gap belongs to another Topic, hand it off explicitly rather than duplicating research.
8\. Research closure means \*\*everything actionable at the current stage is complete and remaining work is explicitly deferred/handed off\*\*. It does not mean literature exhaustion, production accuracy, or architecture approval.
9\. For new academic work, use terminology refinement, strict paper admission, manual/controlled canonical acquisition, corpus freeze, fresh isolated Pipeline runs, direct-vs-transfer labels, independent review, strict validation, and post-round gap review. These are lessons learned from Topics 01 and 02.
10\. For engineering research, keep gold independent from the component under test; structurally separate prediction inputs from evaluation gold/future context; count false positives and false negatives in end-to-end denominators; use clean-workspace reproducibility, mutation/regression tests, and fresh independent methodological review.

    Studies sentence-level question-answer pairing in asynchronous email conversations. The method uses email-thread structure together with lexical and contextual features to identify which earlier question an answer addresses, providing direct empirical evidence for non-adjacent reply alignment in email.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-1609-aaai-v33i01-3301134\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Learning to Align Question and Answer Utterances in Customer Service Conversation with Recurrent Pointer Networks (2019, AAAI 2019)
    Directly models question-answer utterance alignment in multi-round customer-service conversations. A recurrent pointer network exploits conversational context and dependencies among alignments and accommodates empty as well as multiple alignments, providing empirical evidence for responses that do not map one-to-one to prior questions.
\- paper\_id \`manual-a2970abe9c\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Forst: A Challenge to the NTCIR-16 QA Lab-PoliInfo-3 Task (2022, Proceedings of the 16th NTCIR Conference on Evaluation of Information Access Technologies)
    Presents a system for the NTCIR-16 Question Answer Alignment task. It segments questioner and answerer statements and maps individual questions to answers using lexical-overlap and embedding-based information, with alignment directly evaluated against the task gold standard.

    Targets meeting transcripts in which a participant may ask several questions together and officials subsequently answer the corresponding questions one by one. A two-stage method segments question and answer material and then aligns corresponding units, explicitly addressing multiple competing prior questions rather than assuming adjacency.

    Integrates automatically detected question-answer pairs into extractive summaries of email conversations and evaluates their contribution to summary quality. It provides indirect empirical validation that identifying cross-message question-answer relations captures salient structure in email threads.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-1016-j-pragma-2007-07-011\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Multiple questions in oral proficiency interviews (2007, Journal of Pragmatics)
    Analyzes more than one hundred question/task instances in oral proficiency interviews and documents turns containing multiple questions. It distinguishes different organizations of repeated or multiple questioning and examines how these arise around repair, missing rejoinders, and problematic answers, providing empirical evidence that response scope cannot always be inferred from the immediately preceding question alone.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-20736-0002002282\` [identity: UNCHECKED] ditlab at the NTCIR-16 QA Lab-PoliInfo-3 (2022, Proceedings of the 16th NTCIR Conference on Evaluation of Information Access Technologies)
    Implements question-answer alignment for governmental assembly minutes by identifying related sentence or paragraph units and comparing questions with candidate answers through several matching features. The output explicitly associates earlier questions with later answers rather than merely labeling dialogue acts.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-20736-0002002284\` [identity: UNCHECKED] AKBL at the NTCIR-16 QA Lab-PoliInfo-3 Task (2022, Proceedings of the 16th NTCIR Conference on Evaluation of Information Access Technologies)
    Addresses Question Answer Alignment in assembly minutes where questions and answers may be presented in batches without explicit correspondence. The system segments question and answer texts into semantically coherent units and uses BM25-based scores with a Hungarian-algorithm assignment to align them.

    Defines an evaluated Question Answer Alignment task over Japanese assembly minutes. The task extracts topical ranges and correspondences between questions and responses in collective-questioning settings where several questions and answers can occur in batches, supplying independently defined gold and formal system evaluation for alignment.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-1016-j-ipm-2023-103613\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Hierarchical graph fusion network and a new argumentative dataset for multiparty dialogue discourse parsing (2024, Information Processing & Management)
    Studies discourse parsing for multiparty argumentative dialogue, where relationships must be extracted between conversational discourse units. It introduces manually annotated argumentative dialogue datasets and a hierarchical graph-fusion model that combines contextual information to predict discourse structure, providing additional empirical evidence for nonlocal target attachment.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-3233-aic-2012-0516\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Detection of imperative and declarative question–answer pairs in email conversations (2012, AI Communications)
    Extends email question-answer detection beyond interrogative sentences to imperative and declarative forms. The sentence-level model uses content, context, and thread-structure features and is evaluated on benchmark email corpora, making it directly relevant to replies that answer requests or propositions not syntactically marked as questions.
\- paper\_id \`manual-be69c3aa17\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Annotating Abstract Pronominal Anaphora in the DAD Project (2008, LREC 2008)
    Presents an annotation scheme for abstract pronominal anaphora in texts and dialogues. Antecedents may be verb phrases, clauses, or larger discourse segments, and the paper reports inter-coder evaluation, providing empirical support for span-based annotation of proposition-like antecedents.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-18653-v1-2023-eacl-main-247\` [identity: UNCHECKED] A simple but effective model for attachment in discourse parsing with multi-task learning for relation labeling (2023, EACL 2023)
    Uses a BERT-based pair encoder to predict discourse attachments while jointly learning discourse-relation labels. Importantly for multi-proposition response scope, the representation permits a discourse node to have multiple parents, an empirically relevant property of multiparty conversation that is lost under single-antecedent tree assumptions.
\- paper\_id \`manual-7743c50805\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Identifying reference to abstract objects in dialogue (2006, 10th Workshop on the Semantics and Pragmatics of Dialogue (BRANDIAL 2006))
    Reports annotation experiments in which annotators identify antecedents for discourse-deictic expressions as unconstrained regions of dialogue text. Annotators show convergence on the identity of abstract antecedent regions, supporting empirical span-based treatment of propositions and discourse segments instead of restricting targets to noun phrases.

    Studies English Reddit conversations annotated for speech acts and functional-dependence relations connecting discourse segments to preceding material. The analysis relates informational exchanges, answers and clarification requests, and explicit agreement or disagreement to different degrees of subjectivity, providing recent empirical data with explicit response dependencies.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-18653-v1-s15-1035\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Resolving Discourse-Deictic Pronouns: A Two-Stage Approach to Do It (2015, Fourth Joint Conference on Lexical and Computational Semantics (\*SEM 2015))
    Presents a two-stage system that first detects discourse-deictic pronouns and then resolves them to verbal or clausal antecedents. The empirical evaluation separates detection from antecedent resolution and demonstrates a computational approach to proposition-like target selection beyond entity coreference.
\- paper\_id \`manual-e4d6ad7ca1\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Anaphoric Annotation in the ARRAU Corpus (2008, LREC 2008)
    Describes anaphoric annotation in ARRAU, which includes task-oriented dialogue among its genres. The representation explicitly permits multiple antecedents for ambiguous expressions and discourse antecedents denoting abstract entities such as events, actions, and plans, making it useful for null, ambiguity, and multi-antecedent modeling.
\- paper\_id \`manual-f6b3355bcf\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Clarifying Intentions in Dialogue: A Corpus Study (2015, 11th International Conference on Computational Semantics (IWCS 2015))
    Presents a corpus-based investigation of clarification requests concerning interlocutor intentions. It distinguishes problems of intention recognition from problems of intention adoption and conducts an annotation experiment on naturally occurring candidate clarification sequences, providing empirical evidence about what a clarification targets.
\- paper\_id \`manual-1e515febba\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Resolving Discourse Deictic Anaphora in Dialogues (1999, EACL 1999)
    Presents an algorithm for resolving discourse-deictic anaphora in spoken dialogue. It first distinguishes individual, discourse-deictic, and vague uses of pronouns and demonstratives and then resolves discourse-deictic cases against preceding discourse, with empirical evaluation on spoken-dialogue data.
\- paper\_id \`manual-2ce01eecee\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Resolving Demonstrative Anaphora in the TRAINS93 Corpus (1998, 2nd Colloquium on Discourse, Anaphora and Reference Resolution)
    Reports empirical annotation and analysis of third-person pronouns and demonstratives in task-oriented TRAINS93 dialogue. The study distinguishes ordinary entity reference from demonstratives whose referents are plans or larger discourse material and motivates a resolver capable of handling both kinds of antecedent.
\- paper\_id \`manual-14f72b0c0b\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Discourse Structure and Dialogue Acts in Multiparty Dialogue: the STAC Corpus (2016, LREC 2016)
    Introduces the STAC corpus of multi-party strategic chats annotated with full SDRT discourse structures. The data contain interleaved conversational threads and explicit discourse links between elementary discourse units, supplying empirical material for evaluating non-local response attachment rather than only turn-level dialogue acts.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-3115-1117736-1117743\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Abstract Anaphora Resolution in Danish (2000, 1st SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue)
    Studies Danish pronouns and deictic expressions that can refer either to individuals or to abstract discourse objects. An adapted resolution algorithm is evaluated on four dialogues drawn from two dialogue collections, providing empirical evidence for dialogue-level abstract antecedent selection.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-1007-s10489-013-0481-1\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Towards identifying unresolved discussions in student online forums (2014, Applied Intelligence)
    Empirically analyzes discussion structures in student online forums to identify unresolved discussions and unanswered questions. The work distinguishes patterns in which questions receive answers from those in which issues remain unresolved, making it relevant to explicit modeling of missing response links.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-18653-v1-d15-1109\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Discourse parsing for multi-party chat dialogues (2015, EMNLP 2015)
    Develops a discourse parser for multi-party chat that predicts discourse attachments and relation labels among elementary discourse units. Because the parser must decide which preceding discourse unit a new unit attaches to in threaded and interleaved dialogue, it provides direct computational evidence for response-antecedent selection below the whole-message level.
\- paper\_id \`doi-10-1093-jos-17-1-51\` [identity: UNCHECKED] Dialogue Acts, Synchronizing Units, and Anaphora Resolution (2000, Journal of Semantics)
    Reports a corpus analysis and a model of anaphora resolution in spontaneous spoken dialogue. The analysis distinguishes nominal antecedents from sentential or discourse-deictic antecedents and from vague cases with no clearly identifiable linguistic antecedent, directly motivating null or unresolved outcomes rather than forced nearest-antecedent attachment.
